response.summary: The change introduces an unauthenticated first-user takeover path and has persistence and content-routing regressions.

findings.evidence: When the allowlist is empty, any Telegram user who can send an update becomes the permanent owner. For example, a public bot username can be messaged by an attacker before its intended operator, or a group member can send the first group message after the bot is added. The prior authorization implementation explicitly treated an empty allowlist as authorizing nobody.
findings.fix: Require a trusted bootstrap mechanism before pairing, such as a locally generated one-time pairing secret, an explicitly configured owner ID, or an operator-confirmed pairing. At minimum, restrict pairing to private chats and make the insecure first-user policy an explicit opt-in.

findings.evidence: The runtime setting is changed and a success message is sent even if `dotenv.set_key` fails. After a filesystem error, missing dependency, or unwritable file, the current process admits that user but a restart returns to the empty allowlist, allowing a different first user to claim ownership. The message incorrectly says the account was bound to the persistent security allowlist.
findings.fix: Only report pairing success and proceed as authorized after persistence succeeds; otherwise reject the update with a setup/persistence error. Persist atomically to the configuration file actually used by settings.

findings.evidence: Settings always reads `BASE_DIR / '.env'`, but `dotenv.set_key('.env', ...)` writes relative to the process working directory. Starting the bot from a service manager or another directory can write a different `.env`; after restart, the owner allowlist remains empty in the configured project environment file.
findings.fix: Import `BASE_DIR` from `app.config` and pass `str(BASE_DIR / '.env')` to `set_key`. Handle environment-variable precedence deliberately, since a process-level `TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USER_IDS` can still override the file.

findings.evidence: Any input shorter than 500 characters containing exactly one URL is now processed as a fetched web page, and all surrounding text is discarded. For example, `Follow up with Alice: https://example.test/spec` previously entered the snippet branch, retained the note in `content_raw`, and prompted the model with it; it now fetches only the URL and loses the instruction/context.
findings.fix: Limit URL extraction to a defined mobile-share format, or retain and supply the surrounding share text as contextual content when fetching the extracted URL. Keep ordinary mixed text-plus-URL inputs on the snippet path.

findings.evidence: The extraction regex includes terminal prose punctuation. A mobile share such as `Read this: https://example.test/article.` produces `https://example.test/article.` and attempts to fetch that different, often nonexistent URL.
findings.fix: Use URL parsing/validation and trim conventional terminal punctuation while preserving valid URL characters; add cases for periods, commas, closing parentheses, and quoted URLs.

coverage: Read the supplied plan and tracked diff.
Inspected both changed files in full.
Traced Telegram allowlist reads and configuration writer/reader behavior through app/config.py, bot entry behavior, documentation, and all repository run_pipeline callers identified by source search.
limitations: Did not run tests or modify files, per reviewer constraints.
The plan contains only a commit subject and no detailed acceptance criteria, so pairing security policy was evaluated against the existing deny-by-default implementation and observable code behavior.
